full_judgment:
2. The plaintiff-appellant filed the aforesaid money suit alleging inter alia, that one MA Nasir, husband of defendant-respondent No. 1 and father of defendant-respondent Nos. 2 to 4, got an allotment of 19 katha 15 chataks of land at Road No. 53, Block No. NW (J) Gulshan Model Town Dhaka from former DIT now RAJUK by way of permanent lease for construction of pucca residential house thereon. Said MA Nasir obtained loan of Taka. 40,000.00 from East Pakistan House Building Finance Corporation for constructing his house thereon. But said MA Nasir failed to repay the said loan. Accordingly, House Building Finance Corporation filed Miscellaneous Case No. 88 of 1976 under Article 27 of PO 7 of 1973 for recovery of Taka. 59,653.00 and obtained an ex parte decree. In execution of the said decree the property mentioned in the schedule to the plaint was auction-sold to the plaintiff-appellant for a consideration of Taka. 34,62,500.00. The plaintiff-appellant was thereafter given a sale certificate. The defendants-respondents resisted the plaintiff-appellant to take over possession of the property by filing a petition in the said Money Execution Case No. 7 of 1978 before District Judge, Dhaka for substituting their names in place of MA Nasir but without any success. Hence, defendant-respondents filed Title Suit No. 555 of 1985 in the First Court of the Subordinate Judge, Dhaka which was subsequently renumbered as Title Suit No. 269 of 1987 and the same was also dismissed. The defendant-respondents thereafter preferred First Appeal No. 46 of 1988 before the High Court Division. The said appeal was also dismissed with observation that defendant-respondents as legal heirs of said MA Nasir would be entitled to receive the sale proceeds after payment of legal dues to the House Building Finance Corporation. High Court Division also detected the defendant-respondents to quit the suit house within three months. In this background of the case, the defendant-respondents filed Civil Appeal No. 68 of 1989 before the, Appellate Division which was also dismissed on 15-3-90. The Appellate Division while dismissing the appeal gave one month''s time to the defendant-respondents for vacating the suit house. Defendant-respondents, thereafter, filed a petition in the aforesaid execution case which was also rejected by the District Judge after hearing. Thereafter Civil Revision No. 2589 of 1990 was filed in the High Court Division by defendant-respondents which was also rejected. Against such rejection, defendant-respondents went up to the Appellate Division by filing a leave petition in which leave was granted and ultimately appeal was dismissed by the Appellate Division as not pressed. In this background of the litigations, the plaintiff- appellant filed the present suit claiming Taka 5,40,000.00 as rents of the suit house for three years at the rate of Taka. 15,000.00 per month. The plaintiff-appellant also claimed various amounts on account of mental anxiety, loss of sleep, litigation expenses incurred by her including Taka 8 (eight) lakh as transfer fees paid by her in favour of RAJUK. The plaintiff-appellant, therefore, filed the present suit claiming a total amount of Taka 18 lakh from the defendant-respondents by way of compensation. 

 2. Whether the plaintiff is entitled to get Taka 5,40,000.00 as total rents at monthly rate of Taka 15,000.00 from 18-1-87 to 28-2-91, Taka 25,000.00 as expenses incurred in Money Execution Case No. 7 of 1978, Taka. 1,35,000.00 as expenses incurred in Title Suit No. 269 of 1987, Taka. 2,50,000.00 as expenses incurred in the High Court Division and Appellant Division, Taka 25,000.00 for mental tension, Taka 25,000.00 for having no sleep and Taka 8 (eight) lakh as transfer fee. 

 7. Md. Nurul Huq, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-appellant, argues that the plaintiff-appellant being a bonafide purchaser of the suit property for value was harassed by the defendant-respondents by filing frivolous and vexatious cases after she purchased and obtained sale certificate in respect of the suit property. Because of such vexatious litigations the plaintiff-appellant had not only to spend a huge amount by way of court-fees, Advocate fees, house rents, etc., but she also suffered from mental agony and insomnia including loss of earnings by way of house rent in respect of the suit house which she purchased on auction-sale through Court and, as such, she was entitled to be compensated for such loss and sufferings. But the trial Court having failed to appreciate this position dismissed the suit and thus committed an illegality. The learned Advocate further submits that the trial Court also erred in failing to hold that the defendant-respondents were under an obligation to pay the transfer fee to RAJUK for transfer of the suit house as they are going to enjoy the sale proceeds. 

 8. Mr. AF Hassan Arif, the learned Advocate for the defendant-respondents, on the other hand submits that since the plaintiff-respondents had to file the cases in order to safeguard and protect their interest there was no warrant in law or in fact for the defendant-respondents to compensate the defendant-appellant for filing those cases. 

 9. The question that falls for determination is whether the cases complained of and in relation to which the plaintiff-appellant filed the instant suit for compensation are frivolous and vexatious civil proceedings causing damage to her reputation, person, freedom or property. In other words, it is important to find out whether the defendants-respondents commenced those legal proceedings with the honest intention of protecting their own interest. 

 10. It is found that the defendant-respondents having learnt about Execution Case No. 7 of 1979 filed application to resist the same by substituting them as heirs of MA Nasir. But being unsuccessful they (defendant-respondents) filed Title Suit No. 269 of 1987 with the following prayer : 

 (b) that a decree declaring that the decree order passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 88 of 1976 on 21-9-77 is illegal, null and void being obtained against a dead man by practicing fraud upon the Court and by suppressing process of the Court; 

 11. The trial Court dismissed the above suit on the ground that the suit was time-barred and not maintainable and that the predecessor-in-interest of the defendant-respondents MA Nasir was alive. On appeal from the said judgment (Fist Appeal No. 46 of 1988) a Division Bench of the High Court Division by the judgment and decree dated 16-2-89 decreed the suit with only one declaration that the plaintiffs were the sole legal heirs and successors of late MA Nasir and that they were entitled to the sale-proceeds of the suit property minus the dues of the House Building Finance Corporation. The High Court Division by the said judgment also allowed the defendant respondents to stay in the suit house for 3 months from the date of drawing up of the decree in the appeal. On an appeal being, Civil Appeal No. 68 of 1989 filed by the defendant-respondents against the above judgment the Appellate Division by judgment dated 15-3-90 upheld the said judgment of the High Court Division. Thereafter, the defendant-respondents filed an application in the aforesaid Money Execution Case No. 7 of 1987 for setting aside the auction-sale on the ground that the plaintiff-appellant failed to deposit the entire auction money within the statutory period. On rejection of the said prayer by the Execution Court, the defendant-respondents filed Civil Revision No. 2589 of 1990. But the same was dismissed by the High Court Division by judgment dated 22-11-90. The defendant-respondents thereafter challenged the said judgment before the Appellate Division by filing Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 7 of 1991 which was eventually dismissed as not pressed with the direction that the defendant-respondents would not be evicted from the suit property before expiry of 1 month from date. 

 13. In the case of Bahori Lal vs. Sri Ram reported in AIR 1946 All. 139 it is held that generally speaking, it is not an actionable wrong to institute civil proceedings without reasonable and probable cause even if malice is established. The law allows every person to employ its process for the purpose of asserting his rights without subjecting him to any liability other than the liability to pay the costs of the proceedings. 

 15. In the case of Ramdeo vs. Messers B Chand regarding attachment before judgment reported in AIR 1962 Raj 164 it was held that an action for damages based on malicious abuse of civil process is analogous to an action for malicious prosecution and in such cases the plaintiff must allege and prove malice and that the defendant acted without reasonable and probable cause, apart from showing that the proceedings ultimately terminated in his favour. 

 17. It is found from the judgments and orders of the trial Court, High Court Division and the Appellate Division that the defendant-respondents filed the cases complained of with bonafide belief that they had good cause of action and they, would succeed in getting relief. In other words, the civil proceedings complained of were commenced by the defendant-respondents with a view to protecting their interest and, as such, they were not vexatious proceedings. 

 18. In the present case the plaintiff-appellant prayed for compensation for alleged damage to her property only and not for any damage to her person or reputation stating that she was forced to spend her money to defend those vexatious civil suits and proceedings. PWs 1, 2 and 3 merely state in their depositions that the plaintiff-appellant spent money in the aforesaid litigations, lost earnings by way of rents and she also suffered from mental anxiety, etc. But the plaintiff-appellant could not bring any specific and concrete proof as to the amount she spent by way of litigation expenses and also as to the amount she lost by way of income as rents of the suit house. 

 19. Since it is found that the cases complained of were not vexatious the instant suit claiming compensation was rightly dismissed by the trial Court more so when the plaintiff-appellant failed to prove any damage to her property. 

 "23 That subject to provisions of Clause 22 of these presents the LESSEE may, after full payment of the total premium has been made and after completing the construction of the ground floor of residential building as per plan approved by the Authorized Officer, DIT transfer the whole of the demised property but not part of it, on giving clear 30 (thirty) days'' notice in writing to the lessor and after obtaining the prior permission of the lessor in writing and on prior payment to the lessor of a transfer fee which shall constitute a prior charge on the demised property and which for all transfers taking place before the Thirty First day of December, 1987 shall be at the rate of Taka 20 lacs per bigha of the demised property and for transfer taking place thereafter the transfer fee shall be at the rate to be fixed from time to time by the Lessor" PW 4 Habibullah, a Superintendent of RAJUK stated in his deposition that the transfer fee is required to be paid at the rate of Taka 8 (eight) lakh per bigha if it is sold at Taka 20(twenty) lakh or more per bigha. From the cl reading of the aforesaid Clause it appears that the defendant-respondents as lessees are liable to pay transfer fee if the transfer is made by them. Since the transfer in question is not made by the defendant-respondents but by Court at the instance of House Building Finance Corporation in execution of a decree the defendant-respondents are not liable to pay the transfer fee in this case.
